Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn these notes into a clear prompt for planning a family photo archive setup? this is for the Bell family, mostly Nia Bell and her brother Mateo, and not a business archive. They have folders going back to their grandparents’ albums, plus newer phone pictures. Please ask for a practical setup plan that helps them keep one reliable family collection without pretending they have already chosen a particular app or storage company. I don't want the response to configure anything for them or act like the choices are already settled.

Nia has done most of the scanning in the dining room. Mateo handles the shared family drive and wants a way to keep the originals protected while still letting relatives find and view pictures. Aunt Lila, their mother, and two cousins should be able to browse the collection, but only Nia and Mateo should be described as editing the originals. The cousins may send additions for review; don't turn that into permission for them to change the main archive. Their family is spread across three households, and not everyone has the same phone or computer. They want the plan to address access from those households, but keep it understandable for relatives who aren't technical.

Keep these remarks exactly as written, as context the person making the plan should consider: Nia said, “I want the scans to stay readable, but I don't want every cousin editing the originals.” Mateo said, “If Aunt Lila asks us to remove a picture, we need to know which copies are affected.” They are ordinary family comments, not settled technical specifications. Aunt Lila sometimes remembers who is in old pictures, and she has offered to add names and approximate dates when she can. Don't present those dates as certain if nobody knows them.

The material they have is mixed. The dining-room scanner exports TIFF files at 600 dpi; phone photos arrive as HEIC or JPEG. There are also a few older JPEG scans from a cousin, but Nia does not know whether those were resized. Some albums have handwritten captions and the original order matters. In one album a photo has a note on the back identifying a school picnic, but no year. Ask that the plan cover keeping useful information such as captions, dates when known, people names, and album sequence, and distinguish guesses from known details. They don't want an approach that silently strips those details when making viewing copies. Please keep the original scans and camera files in scope rather than suggesting that viewing copies replace them.

A source note from Nia reads: “The dining-room scanner exports TIFF files at 600 dpi; phone photos arrive as HEIC or JPEG.” Another note from Mateo reads: “We have one external drive at my apartment and a second copy on the family drive, but I have not checked every folder against the other.” Keep those notes exactly as written. They want the plan to discuss a way of checking for missing or duplicate files and explaining what to do when two files look alike but may not be identical. Don't imply they have already verified either copy. They are not asking for a restoration project or a new round of scanning; the request is about arranging, protecting, and sharing what they already have, while noting the uncertainty about the older scans.

There is a concern about remote access. Mateo prefers the family drive to be reachable by relatives when they are away from home, but Nia is not sure that every folder should be remotely available. Don't resolve that disagreement for them or present remote access as already approved. They also want to understand whether a local copy can remain available if the internet is down. The actual choice of services, device models, and network settings is open. The setup plan should explain the choices they need to make without assuming a particular product, and it should keep the distinction between a local copy and any remote access clear.

Include this exact configuration material as one of the inputs to consider, without editing its wording or values:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 24
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

They haven't said whether the 24-day retention value applies to deleted items, version history, or something else, so ask the planner to flag that meaning as something to clarify rather than deciding it. Also make clear that the value shown for remote access is part of this material, not evidence that the family has chosen a final remote-access policy. This uncertainty matters alongside Mateo's preference and Nia's hesitation, so don't flatten the three things into a single settled rule.

Please organize the prompt so the resulting plan covers the family’s goals, roles and permissions, importing and naming files, preserving captions and sequence, protecting original files, maintaining and checking copies, browsing and sharing across households, and unresolved questions. Ask for steps the family can realistically follow and for an explanation of tradeoffs in plain language, not a sales pitch. It should avoid assuming expertise, inventing dates or permissions, or treating uncertain metadata as fact. Keep the result focused on this one family and the material described above, and don't ask the planner to choose an app on the family's behalf.

One condition that needs to remain visible is this: if a relative asks to exclude a particular photo before it is added to the shared collection, the plan should describe how the family can hold that item aside while they clarify the request; it should not assume that the photo is deleted everywhere or that the request applies to other pictures. Mateo's question about tracing affected copies is relevant if they later ask to remove an image already included. Those are different situations. The final prompt should keep that distinction and ask for a clear way to identify where an included image has copies, without claiming that such tracking already exists.

At the end, include a brief section asking the planner to list the decisions still needed from Nia and Mateo, including the meaning of the retention value, what should be available remotely, who can submit or approve additions, and how approximate dates or names should be recorded. They may consult Aunt Lila on identifications, but don't make her responsible for technical administration. Close with a request for a practical, staged plan that can begin with their existing files and current copies, says where the family's information is still incomplete, and leaves product and access decisions open for them to make.", "output": "Create a practical setup plan for the Bell family’s photo archive, based on the details below. The archive is for family use, not business use. Focus on arranging, protecting, and sharing the material they already have; do not configure anything, assume decisions have been made, or turn the request into a scanning or restoration project. Do not choose an app, storage company, or product on the family’s behalf.

## Family, goals, and access

Nia Bell has done most of the scanning in the dining room. Her brother Mateo manages the shared family drive. Their mother, Aunt Lila, and two cousins should be able to browse and view the collection, while only Nia and Mateo should edit the originals. Cousins may submit additions for review, but that does not give them permission to change the main archive. The family is spread across three households and uses different phones and computers. Explain access across those households in language that nontechnical relatives can understand.

Keep these family remarks exactly as written and treat them as context, not settled technical specifications. Nia said, “I want the scans to stay readable, but I don't want every cousin editing the originals.” Mateo said, “If Aunt Lila asks us to remove a picture, we need to know which copies are affected.” Aunt Lila has offered to add names and approximate dates to older photos when she can remember them. Do not present uncertain dates as certain.

## Existing files and information

The collection includes folders going back to the grandparents’ albums, newer phone pictures, and a few older JPEG scans from a cousin. Nia does not know whether those older scans were resized. The dining-room scanner exports TIFF files at 600 dpi; phone photos arrive as HEIC or JPEG. Some albums have handwritten captions, and the original order matters. One photo has a note on the back identifying a school picnic but giving no year.

Ask the plan to cover importing and naming files, and preserving useful information such as captions, dates when known, people’s names, and album sequence. Distinguish guesses from known details. Do not silently strip useful information when making viewing copies, and do not suggest that viewing copies replace the original scans and camera files.

Keep these source notes exactly as written:
“The dining-room scanner exports TIFF files at 600 dpi; phone photos arrive as HEIC or JPEG.”
“We have one external drive at my apartment and a second copy on the family drive, but I have not checked every folder against the other.”

The plan should discuss how to check for missing or duplicate files, and what to do when two files look alike but may not be identical. Do not imply that either existing copy has already been verified.

## Copies, local storage, and remote access

Mateo prefers relatives to be able to reach the family drive when away from home. Nia is unsure whether every folder should be remotely available. Do not resolve that disagreement or present remote access as approved. Explain whether and how a local copy could remain available if the internet is down, keeping local storage distinct from remote access. Device models and network settings are open choices.

Consider this configuration material without changing its wording or values:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 24
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

The family has not said whether the 24-day retention value applies to deleted items, version history, or something else. Flag its meaning for clarification rather than deciding it. The remote-access value in the material is not evidence that the family has adopted a final remote-access policy. Keep that uncertainty visible alongside Mateo’s preference and Nia’s hesitation.

## Handling requests about individual photos

If a relative asks to exclude a particular photo before it is added to the shared collection, describe how the family can hold that item aside while clarifying the request. Do not assume it has been deleted everywhere or that the request applies to other pictures. Distinguish this situation from a request to remove an image that is already included. In the latter case, Mateo’s question about tracing affected copies is relevant. Ask for a clear way to identify where an included image has copies without claiming that such tracking already exists.

## Decisions and plan format

Organize the plan around the family’s goals, roles and permissions, importing and naming files, preserving captions and sequence, protecting originals, maintaining and checking copies, browsing and sharing across households, and unresolved questions. Explain tradeoffs in plain language, avoid a sales pitch, and propose steps the family can realistically follow. Do not invent dates or permissions, treat uncertain metadata as fact, or assume technical expertise.

End with a brief list of decisions still needed from Nia and Mateo, including what the retention value means, what should be available remotely, who may submit or approve additions, and how approximate names or dates should be recorded. Aunt Lila may help identify people, but should not be made responsible for technical administration. Provide a practical, staged plan that can start with the existing files and current copies, identify where information is incomplete, and leave product and access decisions open for the family to make."}]
